name: Crowns and bridges
lead: A dental crown is a cap that fully covers or encircles a natural tooth or an implant, and a dental bridge is a fixed prosthesis that replaces one or more missing teeth by joining an artificial tooth (a pontic) to neighbouring teeth or implants [1][2]. In appearance terms, crowns rebuild the shape, size, colour and position of a broken, worn, discoloured or misshapen tooth, and bridges close gaps in the smile, so both restore the look of a complete, even row of teeth [1][8].

Crowns are used for badly broken or worn teeth, to strengthen heavily restored teeth, to finish root canal treatment, to cover the visible part of a single implant, and to improve the look of teeth that simpler cosmetic procedures cannot fix [1]. Materials range from gold and other metal alloys through porcelain-fused-to-metal to all-ceramic options such as lithium disilicate and zirconia, with ceramics chosen mainly for appearance [1][2].

Both are long-established parts of restorative dentistry and are also sold as cosmetic treatments alongside whitening, bonding, veneers and implants [8]. Reference works report high medium-term survival for modern restorations, with typical complications including decay at the margins, porcelain chipping and debonding [1][2]. Preparing a tooth for a crown, or the abutment teeth for a conventional bridge, permanently removes tooth structure, a trade-off that dentists and patients weigh against alternatives such as veneers, bonding and implants [1][8][16]. Dental tourism, especially to destinations offering low-cost veneers and crowns, has made the procedures a topic of wider public discussion [17].

paras: Dentists list several reasons for a crown: replacing a failed crown, restoring a badly worn, broken or fractured tooth that a filling cannot rebuild, strengthening an extensively restored tooth, covering a root-treated tooth, covering the visible part of a single implant, and improving appearance when cosmetic procedures are not enough [1]. Crowns on root-treated teeth were long routine, although recent reviews cited in the reference literature find no strong evidence that they outperform other restorations, so the decision rests on clinical judgement and patient preference; crowns are generally considered justified when the access cavity spans more than a third of the chewing surface or when tooth walls are undermined [1].

Bridges address missing teeth. A bridge keeps the arch looking continuous, and the pontic can be shaped and shaded to match neighbouring teeth. Assessment before treatment looks at gum and pulp health, decay risk, bite, remaining tooth structure, tooth height and root shape, and the patient's aesthetic expectations and commitment to oral hygiene [1][2].

Crowns may be full or partial coverage and are typically made outside the mouth, then cemented. Three-quarter and seven-eighths crowns preserve more tooth but are technically demanding and can show metal in the smile, so they are rarely used [1]. Preparation shapes the tooth to retain the crown while preserving as much structure as possible, with the finish line (margin) ideally placed above the gumline on enamel, and a ferrule of healthy tooth encircling a root-treated tooth is described as reducing fracture risk. A temporary crown protects the tooth, holds the bite and maintains appearance while the final crown is made [1].

Impressions are traditionally taken in silicone, while digital scans are described as about as accurate and more comfortable. Chairside CAD/CAM systems can design and mill a ceramic crown in one visit, in about 20 minutes without a conventional impression, though the milling equipment costs roughly $100,000 so in-office crowns often cost slightly more than laboratory ones [1]. Reviews describe digital design and manufacturing, including 3D printing, as transforming dental laboratory work [3][4][5].

Full metal crowns are cast from alloys. Gold alloys are durable, need minimal tooth reduction and wear similarly to enamel; palladium alloys, introduced in the 1970s, offered a cheaper option; base-metal alloys are strong but harder to adjust and can wear opposing teeth, and nickel-containing ones can trouble people with nickel allergy [1]. Because metal is visible, it is mostly used at the back of the mouth [1].

Ceramic crowns are chosen mainly for aesthetics but are brittle. Silica-based porcelains look very natural but are weak and are often layered over stronger cores; alumina cores were introduced in 1989; lithium disilicate is translucent and can look grey unless carefully shaded, and the colour of the underlying tooth affects the result [1]. Zirconia is described as the strongest dental material, milled by computer. In monolithic form it is more opaque, so many dentists avoid it on front teeth, while veneered zirconia looks more natural but the veneering porcelain can chip [1]. Laboratory research has examined zirconia's chemical stability and low-temperature ageing [6]. Porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns bond ceramic to a metal core and combine strength with a tooth-coloured surface [1].

Conventional bridges rely on prepared abutment teeth carrying crowns. Fixed-fixed designs join the pontic rigidly to abutments on both sides and suit longer gaps; cantilever designs attach to one abutment, are conservative and common for front teeth, but limit span length; fixed-movable designs allow slightly misaligned abutments with less tooth reduction [2]. Resin-bonded (Maryland) bridges use metal or other wings bonded to etched enamel with minimal or no preparation, making them conservative but more prone to debonding [2]. Bridges can also be supported by implants [2][7].

Pontic shapes include wash-through, bullet, ridge-lap, modified ridge-lap, ovate and conical forms, each balancing appearance against how easily the area can be cleaned [2]. Materials include noble and base-metal alloys, porcelain-fused-to-metal (long regarded as the benchmark, with metal edges that can show grey at the gumline), acrylic, lithium disilicate (not generally recommended for people who grind their teeth) and zirconia, which tolerates heavy bite forces [2]. A Cochrane review is reported to have found insufficient evidence to show ceramic outperforming metal-ceramic restorations [2].

sections.h: Crowns compared with veneers and other options
paras: A full crown covers all visible and biting surfaces, while a laminate veneer covers only the front surface and is mainly cosmetic. Veneers are thin shells of porcelain or composite resin bonded to the tooth and are described as often looking better and collecting less plaque, with porcelain veneers needing little or no tooth reduction in many cases [18]. Cosmetic dentistry summaries list whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns, bridges, implants, reshaping and gum lifts, and orthodontic straightening as the main routes to changing a smile [8]. Dentist Newell Sill Jenkins (1840-1919), working largely in Dresden, is credited with developing porcelain techniques for inlays, crowns and bridges and is regarded as a founder of aesthetic dentistry [8].

CAD/CAM crowns made from certain blocks were reported as over 95 percent clinically successful at five years and at least 90 percent functioning at ten [1]. Porcelain-fused-to-metal bridges are reported at about 95 percent success over ten years, with survival depending on span length, position, and the number, condition and shape of the abutment teeth; vital teeth are preferred as abutments over root-treated ones, and stable gums and good oral hygiene are prerequisites [2]. Cosmetic dentistry summaries put the average bridge lifespan near ten years, similar to crowns [8].

For crowns, reported problems include pulp irritation or damage during preparation, fracture of root-treated teeth without adequate coverage, gum inflammation, recession or bone loss when margins sit too close to bone, porcelain chipping (especially on zirconia), wear of opposing teeth by some metals and monolithic zirconia, allergy to nickel-containing alloys, and irritation from leftover cement [1]. For bridges, plaque accumulation and gum inflammation are more likely than around single crowns, and failures include decay at the margins, pulp damage, debonding, fractured connectors or veneering, colour mismatch and gum recession; symptoms can include pain, bleeding gums, bad breath and altered taste [2]. Contraindications listed for bridges include heavy bruxism, unstable teeth, poor hygiene and nickel allergy [2].

Tooth reduction for crowns and conventional bridges is irreversible, and cosmetic dentistry sources describe cantilever ('Maryland') bridges for front teeth as having a reputation for failure [8]. Cosmetic dentistry sources also note that the title 'cosmetic dentist' is not a recognised specialty and that some commentators raise concern about general dentists taking on complex full-mouth 'smile makeovers' [8].

Travel for cheaper dentistry is an established part of medical tourism. A porcelain veneer from a Swedish laboratory is cited at about 2,500 Australian dollars in Australia and about 1,200 in India, and clinics in Hungary, Albania, Turkey, Mexico (Los Algodones) and Vietnam serve international patients seeking veneers, crowns and implants [17]. Turkey's regulation on international health tourism took effect on 13 July 2017, and a state agency, USHAS, was set up in 2019 to promote and regulate the sector [17]. The same reference lists risks of treatment abroad as variable aftercare, limited follow-up after returning home, complications that may require extended stays and facilities with weak complaint processes [17].

Registered trials include a prospective clinical study of monolithic zirconia restorations and low-temperature degradation in 101 patients [9], an evaluation of ceramic crowns with two cements [10], a clinical study of zirconia bridges [11], a trial of zirconia-reinforced lithium silicate bridges with different cements [12], a study of wear between enamel and veneered versus monolithic zirconia [13], and an implant study in the upper front jaw [14]. Early work on immediate function of implants in the aesthetic zone [7] and on cemented versus screw-retained suprastructures [15] has also been published.

lore.intro: Crowns, bridges and the wider 'smile makeover' are discussed in appearance communities mainly as routes to straighter, whiter-looking teeth, and as a cost question when treatment abroad is considered.

claims.claim: Ceramic and zirconia crowns look like natural teeth
claims.believers: Clinics and patients choosing tooth-coloured restorations value ceramics for appearance over metal, which can show in the smile [1].
claims.experts: Reference works say ceramics are chosen mainly for aesthetics but are brittle; monolithic zirconia is more opaque, and lithium disilicate can look grey without careful shading [1].

claims.claim: A bridge or crown lasts for many years
claims.believers: Proponents point to success figures such as over 95 percent for certain CAD/CAM crowns at five years [1].
claims.experts: Cosmetic dentistry summaries put bridge lifespan near ten years, with survival depending on span, position and abutment condition [2][8].

claims.claim: Every root-treated tooth needs a crown
claims.believers: Crowns on root-treated teeth were long routine practice [1].
claims.experts: Recent reviews cited in the reference literature find no strong evidence that crowns outperform other restorations on such teeth; clinical judgement decides [1].

claims.claim: Crowns and veneers are a quick route to a 'perfect' smile
claims.believers: Smile-makeover marketing presents crowns and veneers as complete cosmetic solutions [8][18].
claims.experts: Tooth reduction is irreversible; the American Dental Association does not recognise cosmetic dentistry as a specialty; veneers are described as best reserved for appropriate cases [8][18].

claims.claim: Treatment abroad gives the same result for much less money
claims.believers: Patients and clinics cite large price gaps, such as veneers costing about half as much in India as in Australia [17].
claims.experts: Medical tourism sources list variable aftercare, limited follow-up and complaint processes as risks [17].

claims.claim: Resin-bonded (Maryland) bridges are a conservative option
claims.believers: They preserve tooth structure by bonding wings to etched enamel with little or no preparation [2].
claims.experts: They are described as more prone to debonding, and cantilever front-tooth designs have a reputation for failure [2][8].

card.summary: Caps and fixed bridges that rebuild damaged or missing teeth; well-established, but they cost you tooth structure.
card.note: Tooth preparation is irreversible; restorations typically need replacement after about 10 years.

quick.overview:
A crown is a cap that covers a damaged or discoloured tooth. A bridge replaces missing teeth by anchoring an artificial tooth to neighbouring teeth or implants.

They are standard restorative dentistry and are also used cosmetically to improve the look of teeth that whitening or bonding cannot fix.
quick.mechanism: The tooth is shaped, an impression or digital scan is taken, and a restoration made from metal, porcelain or zirconia is cemented on, often designed and milled with CAD/CAM systems.
quick.risks: Preparation permanently removes tooth structure. Reported problems include decay at the margins, porcelain chipping, debonding, gum irritation, wear of opposing teeth and nickel allergy. Typical survival is reported at about 90 to 95 percent over 5 to 10 years.

chain: A damaged, stained or missing tooth is reshaped or replaced by a custom restoration
The restoration is colour-matched and cemented over the tooth or across the gap
A complete, even-looking smile with a natural tooth shape and colour
angle.text: Crowns cover a tooth with a ceramic or metal shell of the chosen shape and shade, and bridges fill a gap with an artificial tooth. Both change what the smile looks like immediately once fitted, and ceramics are chosen mainly for their natural appearance.
